scores.notes: The piece leans so hard on what it can't prove, repeating the same caveats and the 2→9→1 page counts in nearly every section, that the strong contrast between the second and third rewrites gets diluted. It also invents claims the author never made, such as pages being 'customer evidence' and the 'noise from a new system settling in' rationale.

The post says the 40,000 rows were lost in the second incident and that `--rename-map` answers the rename questions ahead of time; the author answers support neither claim, and there is no command example or sample output to show how tidepool works.

The material is strong, but the piece leans on repeated not-X-but-Y turns and tidy one-line section closers, and its ending lesson ('put the lunch on the calendar the day you cancel') feels pre-packaged rather than earned.

The angle is the stock small-room plant post, 'pick the right plants for your light,' and the author's sharpest details, the landlord's remark and the per-plant watering log, are reported flatly instead of carrying the piece.

The piece repeats its one rule and the 2/9/1 pager numbers across several sections and closes with a rule-of-three advice list, so the second half feels padded and formulaic. It also invents details, such as 'I wasn't on that call' and 'didn't open a support ticket', that the author never gave.

The piece repeats the same three numbers four or five times and stacks on meta-commentary ('its shortness is the point', 'I don't think that's a coincidence', the 'common version of this post' setup), so a thin story gets padded to essay length when it needs more scene detail.

The piece keeps disclaiming what it doesn't know (repeated 'I won't invent / can't reconstruct' passages) and repeats the same 2→9 statistic many times, so it feels padded and defensive. Too little of it is spent showing what the four-service diagram actually looked like or what the split concretely involved.

The piece repeats the 2-to-9 page count and the 'nicer diagram' confession at least four times, and the padding of reflexive not-X-but-Y turns ('didn't just undo… it left', 'my rule isn't… my rule is', 'doesn't mean… it means') thins a thin story further.

The piece hedges too much: so many 'I don't remember, so I won't invent it' disclaimers that they crowd out the story, and the essay reads as a meta-commentary on honesty rather than a narrative about billing.

The piece is padded: it repeats the 6am call, the 'nicer diagram' line and the test several times, and it hedges and recaps at length ('I'll let the number speak for itself', the arc summary, the three 'Not...' lines), which dilutes a strong, honest core.

The angle follows the expected Show HN incident-to-tool story, and the post adds unsupported claims: a third-party tool generated the bad SQL, the SQL 'ran cleanly', and someone spent 'an afternoon restoring' the notes. It also never shows a usage example or what the prompt looks like, which leaves the core feature abstract.

The middle section explains a point HN readers already accept (renames are ambiguous) and never shows the actual prompt or a sample `--rename-map` file, so it leans on story instead of showing the tool.

The post needs the real install and diff commands, and their placeholders leave it unpostable. Repeating the 40,000-rows hook in the closing line, plus a neat 'Now it asks.' ending, reads like a pitch rather than a Show HN first comment.
The post never explains how tidepool decides a change might be a rename, and it has no working repo or install line, so HN readers have nothing technical to judge or try.

The drop-plus-add point comes up four or five times, and the paragraph listing what the author can't stand behind reads like a hedge rather than information; a real example of the prompt or the SQL it prints would do more.

The post repeats the author's notes faithfully but adds nothing past the one 40,000-row incident, and 'one question per migration' is an unsupported claim, so the middle reads as a restated thesis rather than new insight.

The ending leans on repeated disclaimers like 「記不清」, 「不確定」 and 「還沒想清楚」, plus a stock closing takeaway, so the trade-off angle loses force; the fixed 'three things' preview and several one-line section closers also feel formulaic.

The piece leans heavily on disclaimers like 「我說不準」「老實說」 and on lines that just restate the author's answers, so the 'who pays the cost' angle feels thin. The closing three-item list and the not-X-but-Y framing also feel formulaic.

The author can't remember any concrete scene, so the piece fills the gap with talk about uncertainty. It repeats the two quotes and says 'I don't know' several times, and the one emotional idea, that people only notice the meeting once it's gone, is stated rather than shown.

The middle sections mostly speculate about what the meeting gave newcomers (who talks, who works with whom, shared frowns), which fills the gap left by thin author material with plausible but generic reasoning, and the ending turns into a stock two-question advice list.

The piece repeats the author's thesis with too many not-X-but-Y reversals and adds person-hour arithmetic (1,260 minutes, 21 hours) that the author never gave, while the one real scene, Xiao Zhou's complaint, has no detail the author could supply.

The piece keeps disclaiming what it can't remember (why the meeting was cut, the scene, how long it had been gone, whether things changed). These repeated meta-hedges, plus a not-X-but-Y frame and a closing refrain line, take up space that concrete detail could fill, so the body reads thin and padded around one good insight.

The piece mostly stitches the author's answers together in order. The monstera detail is the one real tension, and it gets dropped after one line. The ending circles back to the expected 'check your window first' advice, a lesson the piece already stated twice.

The piece lists every author fact as a tidy how-to, with no felt moment or specific failure story, and it invents details to fill the gaps: the landlord pausing at the door, the rod needing no drilled holes, and no longer having to replace pots.
The piece leans on stock not-X-but-Y lines ('不是植物說了算，是你的窗說了算', '不再問…改問…'), adds a closing line that restates the ending, and never shows a single specific plant moment, so it reads like a template.

The piece stays close to the author's answers but lands on the familiar 'pick the right plant first' lesson; the closing advice adds no concrete detail beyond the plant list, the pole and the watering log, which leaves the middle reading like a checklist.
The angle is honest and fits the material, but the piece has no concrete scene, like a fern dying or the first plant that did well, so it reads like a list of lessons instead of a lived story.

The piece keeps announcing what it doesn't remember (cause, fixer, the realization moment, the trigger) and those disclaimers take up whole paragraphs, while tidy closers like 'The diagram never had to answer that call' and the not-X-but-Y lesson sound written to a formula.

The post leans on repeated not-X-but-Y framing: the problem wasn't my care but the wrong purchase, this isn't a guaranteed-easy list, I'm sharing an order not a formula. Apart from the line about the monstera growing one leaf in eight months, it has almost no scenes or details, so it reads as a summary of the takeaway rather than a lived story.

The piece invents two details: that the 40,000 rows were lost 'the second time', and that 'the SQL looked fine and ran cleanly'. Neither appears in the author's answers, and the author said they don't know why their earlier process missed the rename.

The piece repeats its few facts (11 weeks, 2 to 9 pages, the nicer diagram) at least four times and pads them with hedging sections, which dilutes it. It also adds unsupported details like pages landing 'at 3am' and 'broken nights'.

The piece hedges too often: it keeps pointing out what the author doesn't know, and the long 'What I'm still unsure about' section ends weaker than the strong 2-to-9 pages result and the 'pretty in ways I could see, wrong in ways I couldn't' line, which should carry the post.

The piece over-explains its own thesis. It restates the 'one meeting did two jobs' point in several sections, and the tidy three-bullet advice list and moralizing one-line closers weaken the specific material from Ada and 小周.

The piece mostly stitches the author's answers together with little new texture: it shows no example of the prompt and no detail about either incident, so the middle reads like a tidy summary rather than a story.

The middle paragraph repeats the opening's 'asks instead of guessing' point and spends too many sentences hedging about blaming tools; that space could go to concrete details like what the prompt looks like or how the --rename-map file works.

The window-as-selector angle is set up well but stops early: the body goes back to a checklist of the author's facts, and it adds details the author never gave, such as buying ferns because they looked nice, plants crowded near the window, and asking questions in a shop.

The middle and end repeat 'I won't invent what I didn't record' and the one-question check several times, and the closing bullets and fill-in-the-blank template slide into generic advice-post structure that waters down a sharp, honest core.

The line saying the data loss 'came from a tool that guessed wrong' adds a cause the author never gave, and the CI section asks readers to test behavior the author admits they haven't checked, which makes the post feel unfinished.

The piece leans on repeated 'not X, it's Y' framing and short one-line paragraph closers such as '但故事沒停在這裡'. Its closing advice also repeats the same point three times, so the strongest material, Xiao Zhou's remark against the 13/14 submission rate, is diluted by formulaic structure.
文章幾乎只是把作者答案依序改寫一遍，最核心的一句「不是挑好養的，而是挑適合你那扇窗的」又是一個不是X而是Y的句式，而且西曬窗害死蕨類的過程只是概述，缺少能讓人記住的具體場景。

The piece keeps saying what the author doesn't remember or never measured, across the opening, the middle and a whole closing section. The thin story ends up buried under these caveats, and the computed '21 個人小時' adds a number the author never gave.

The middle sections rely on stacked author phrases plus explainer lines like 「小周缺的不是資訊，是位置」 and 「不只是 90 分鐘」, which repeat the thesis instead of adding new scenes. The 小周 moment stays thin and undated, so the turn in the story feels asserted rather than shown.

The body just repeats the angle and the author's main line, so it has no window or plant details beyond the list; the reader has to take the turning point ('問題不在我，也不在植物，是那扇窗') on faith instead of seeing it happen.
這篇幾乎是把作者的回答照順序拼起來：「死了 11 盆蕨類，因為沒先看窗」講了三次，卻沒有一個窗邊的具體畫面或細節，所以讀起來很平。標題也只是把數字列出來，沒把最有力的反轉「別挑好養的」放進去。

The piece hedges about what it doesn't know so often (missing dates, missing war story, missing ask) that the honesty becomes the main texture, and the one sharp lesson gets restated so many times that it loses force.
The piece repeats its uncertainty disclaimers and keeps restating the rule in not-X-but-Y frames, so the middle and the ending drag and lose the punch of the 2→9→1 page numbers.

The rename-ask hook gets repeated three or four times, and the post hedges about what it won't say (detection rule, prompt text, comparisons) without showing a concrete example of the prompt or the SQL. Technical HN readers would want to see that.

The middle of the post keeps going back to what the author doesn't know (the incident details, Migra and Atlas, usage numbers), and the paragraph saying they can't tell the outage story takes space a reader would rather spend on how the rename detection works.

The piece sticks to the author's thin material, so it repeats the line 「資訊可以寫，歸屬感很難寫」 and the 不是X而是Y contrast several times, and it pads short sections with one-line closers and admissions of what the author doesn't remember instead of concrete scenes, which makes it read like a well-built template.
文章幾乎只把作者的回答依序重排，缺少作者自己的細節；「不是X，而是Y」句型和單句收尾段落一再出現，讀起來像模板。

The piece mostly repeats the author's answers in order, with two not-X-but-Y lines and stock closers like「繞了一圈」. Its one strong angle (the 11 dead ferns and copying a plant list won't save you) never gets a concrete scene, so the post reads thin and checklist-like.

The piece copies the author's answers almost line by line in a generic layout: a hook line, an emoji list, then a staged "一定有人會說／其實不是" rebuttal. It has no fern death or moment at the west window shown in scene, so the strong core line rests on a list instead of a story.
The piece keeps repeating the author's admissions of what they don't know and restating the 2-to-9 pages and Ohio facts until they lose force, and the ending falls back on a tidy not-X-but-Y moral.
The angle depends on the Ohio triple charge, which the author can't tie to any rewrite, so the piece keeps restating that gap and padding with repeated not-X-but-Y reversals instead of evidence.

The piece overexplains its own honesty: the repeated 'I can't say / I won't guess' disclaimers and checklist scaffolding bury the strong 11-weeks-vs-3-weeks contrast, and the closer tacks on a not-X-but-Y slogan, an engagement-bait question, and an implied paging trigger for the 2025 merge that the author explicitly declined to claim.

The essay honestly says it doesn't know whether the lunch restored belonging, but it keeps announcing that honesty ("那會是一篇更好讀的文章，但那是編的") and leans on stacked triads; the appended repurposing plan is chatbot residue that also invents details, such as an engineer 'thanking' the author and a two-month timing for 小周.
